1:
The allegory is decoded item by item, and the items do not agree. Pseudo-Jerome gives the fullest key: the vineyard is the house of Israel, the hedge the guardianship of angels, the winefat the law, the tower the temple, the husbandmen the priests, and the fruit obedience. Bede offers alternatives: the hedge is the wall of the city, the winefat the altar. Theophylact makes the hedge the law, which prohibited their mingling with strangers. Henry keeps to tenancy: members of the church are God's tenants, with a good landlord and a good bargain, and the demand was neither hasty nor high.

The servants are identified twice, differently. Bede reads them as the three divisions of the older Scriptures: Moses, whom they angered in the tents; David and the Psalmists, whose songs they despised, asking what portion they had in David; and the prophets, of whom he asks which they did not persecute. Theophylact spaces them by period, the prophets about the time of Elias, when Zedekiah struck Micaiah, then those about Hosea and Isaiah, then those about Daniel. Gill insists no single person is meant but a set of men, the other report having the plural. Ellicott notes the difference of method, that this evangelist sends one servant, then another, then many, where the other divides them into two groups, seizing characteristically on the most vivid presentation. Robertson glosses the verb for wounding in the head, an old word meaning to bring under heads, then to hit on the head, found nowhere else in the New Testament.

Whether the owner really expected reverence is asked by three. Pseudo-Jerome answers that he speaks in irony. Theophylact says it is not spoken as though he were ignorant, but to show what it was right and fitting they should do. Bede extends it to the departure: the going into a far country was not by change of place, but he seemed to go away that he might leave the husbandmen to their own free will, and God is said to doubt for the same reason. Bede refuses the excuse of ignorance, holding that the chiefs crucified not through ignorance but through envy, understanding well who it was that had been promised the heathen for an inheritance.

Augustine takes up a difference between the reports. In the other the hearers answer that he will miserably destroy those wicked men, while here the Lord seems to answer himself; their answer, being true, may have been attributed to him, who gave the same answer concerning them, being the Truth.

On the rejected stone the fathers converge. Bede notices that the men called husbandmen a moment before are now called builders, since those who were to cultivate the people like a vineyard were also to adorn them as a house fit for God; and the corner stone founds the two peoples on himself, building of them one city and one temple. Theophylact makes the same point, that the corner joins Jews and Gentiles, adding that the Church is wonderful as resting upon wonders. Pseudo-Jerome takes the corner as the place where the lamb and the bread met at the supper, ending the Old and beginning the New.

Lightfoot observes that the hearers knew the parable was against them, since the Jews boasted of being the Lord's vineyard and readily noticed any wrong done to it, though not their own unfruitfulness; he adds the rule that a vineyard in its fourth year was marked with coloured clods of earth so that none should eat of it. Bede turns it into a moral: each of the faithful receives a vineyard on hire at baptism, beats the servant when the word is heard and despised, and kills the heir as far as in him lies by trampling on the Son of God; the vineyard passes to another when the humble are enriched with the grace the proud man scorned.
13:
Who the Herodians were is answered two ways. Theophylact reports both, that they were a new sect who held Herod to be the Christ, the succession of Judah having failed, or else Herod's soldiers, brought as witnesses of what Christ said so that they might take him. Henry explains the pairing by their opposite interests: the Pharisees stickled for the liberty of the Jews and the Herodians for the Roman power, so that whichever way he answered, one party could raise the country and the other the governor against him; it is no new thing, he observes, for those at variance in everything else to join in a confederacy against Christ. Theophylact says it in a phrase, that the plot had a precipice on both sides, and the Fountain of wisdom escaped their snares. Bede thinks the question framed to draw the answer that tribute should not be paid, so the Herodians might at once hold him an author of sedition.

The flattery is noticed by all. Pseudo-Jerome compares the questioners to bees, who carry honey in the mouth and a sting in the tail. Henry turns their compliment into evidence: if they meant what they said in calling him true and no respecter of persons, their putting him to death was a sin against knowledge, and out of their own mouths they are judged; if they did not mean it, they flattered him with their tongue. Robertson lays the three reports side by side, this one saying he knew their hypocrisy where the others have wickedness and craftiness, each word a flash-light on the spirit of the questioners, who were sly, shrewd and slick, and did not deceive him with their pious palaver. Ellicott notes that this report uses the specific word for their sin but omits the name hypocrites which the other applies to them; and only here, Robertson adds, is the question repeated in the sharp doubled form, shall we give or shall we not give.

The coin draws out the antiquarian. Lightfoot makes three points: it was a Caesarean penny, and he tells of a heathen who sent one to a rabbi on a feast day of his own, whose colleague advised him to take it and, while the giver watched, drop it down a well; it was silver and not gold, a gold penny being reckoned worth twenty-five silver; and it was Roman, not of Jerusalem, a distinction the rabbis themselves observed. Bede describes it as worth ten smaller coins, and answers those who suppose the question about the image was asked from ignorance: he might have known whose it was, and asked in order to return them a fitting answer.

The answer is applied in three directions. Bede takes the things that are God's to mean tithes, first-fruits, oblations and offerings, and notes that as he paid the tribute for himself and Peter, so he rendered God his own by doing the Father's will. Theophylact reduces it to a rule, that what bears an image goes to him whose image it bears, then extends it unexpectedly: the inevitable wants of our bodies are as Caesar to each of us, so the body is to have its own, food and raiment, and God the things that are God's. Pseudo-Jerome makes the second half the point: we render the money collected for Caesar and render ourselves willingly to God, since it is the light of God's countenance, not Caesar's, that is stamped upon us.

On the closing marvel the notes are brief. Theophylact remarks that those who ought to have believed only wondered, finding no place for their craftiness. Robertson observes the tense, a continuing wonder here where the others have the moment it began, and that one notes they held their peace, the other that they went away.
18:
The questioners come before the question. Theophylact calls them a sect who denied the resurrection and said there was neither angel nor spirit; the Gloss says their fault was to contradict the Scriptures and derogate from the power of God. Henry sharpens the contrast: these were the sceptics of that age, not bigots or persecutors, their design being on the doctrine rather than the person. He thinks the case they put was meant to ridicule the law of the brother's widow and bring the Mosaic frame into contempt, since those who deny divine truths commonly disparage divine laws; and he notes their subtlety, that they do not deny the resurrection outright but appear to own it, as though these beasts of the field were more subtle than the serpent. Bede grants the tale is fitly framed to prove the madness of those who assert the resurrection of the body, though such a thing might really have happened among them.

The answer names two ignorances, both pressed. Robertson notes the reproach is put here as a question expecting assent where the other report makes it a flat assertion, the verb meaning to wander astray; the Sadducees posed as men of superior intelligence, and on this very point were ignorant of the Scriptures, as much error still is among the educated. Theophylact says what the first ignorance was: they supposed a restoration of bodies such as they are now, and it will not be so; and the second, that they thought it hard for scattered limbs to be rejoined to the soul, which is nothing to the divine power.

Why marriage ceases is explained from its purpose. Theophylact says marriage exists now on account of our decay, that we may be carried on by succession and not fail; then we shall be as the angels, who need no succession and never come to an end. Robertson reports that the opposite party held the risen body would perform the functions of marriage and were themselves in error; he passes on the judgment that equality with angels consists in deliverance from mortality, and observes that angels are directly created, not procreated. Barnes adds a limit: the passage teaches that the peculiar relation of marriage will not exist, but does not affirm that there will be no recollection of former marriage, or no recognition of each other as having stood in that relation.

The proof from the bush is handled for its form as much as its force. Barnes explains the manner of citation: when there were no chapters or verses a book was most easily quoted by its subject, as the Jews often did. Ellicott adds that the reference is shared with one other report but missing from the third, and that the word order shows the bush is named not as the place where God spoke but as the title by which that section was known. Theophylact rests the argument on the tense, since he did not say I have been but I am, as though they were present; and answers the objection that only Abraham's soul is meant by replying that the name implies both soul and body. Bede reaches the same end by inference: once the soul is proved to remain, since God could not be God of those who did not exist, the resurrection of the body follows, the body having done good and evil along with the soul.

Pseudo-Jerome reads the whole mystically. The woman who leaves no seed to seven brothers is the synagogue, deserted by the sevenfold Spirit that filled the patriarchs. The bush he makes an image of the hearers, the fire kindled in it not consuming its thorns, as these words set them on fire without burning off the thorns grown under the curse. In the threefold naming of God he finds the Trinity implied, and in the single naming that follows, one substance.
28:
The question had a settled background. Lightfoot explains the rabbinic distinction between the law and the precept, the latter meaning some greater rite such as circumcision or the sabbath, so the question is whether the ceremonial precepts are the greatest, and which stands first; the questioner's own answer prefers the moral law. Bede says the same debate ran between scribes and Pharisees, some praising sacrifices, others preferring acts of faith and love, since many of the fathers before the law pleased God by that faith only which works by love; this man was of the second party. Pseudo-Jerome states the difficulty otherwise, that the commandments are set out differently in Exodus, Leviticus and Deuteronomy, so two rather than one are brought forward, by which, as by two paps on the breast of the bride, our infancy is nourished.

Whether the questioner was sincere the reports themselves dispute. Barnes calls it one of the very few candid inquiries made of him for information. Robertson notes that this report puts the man in a favourable light while the other says he was tempting. Augustine reconciles them twice over: he may have come as a tempter and been corrected by the answer, or the tempting need not be thought evil, being the caution of a man wishing to try a thing unknown to him. Calvin allows the malice and still credits the change, since one who had attacked meaning to take him by surprise not only yields but openly assents, so he does not belong to the class whose obstinacy is incurable; the seed of right knowledge lay choked in his heart.

Theophylact takes the commandment apart by faculties. There is a living power in the soul, to which anger and desire belong; a natural power, to which nutriment and growth belong; and a rational power, called the mind: all are to be given whole to divine love. The Gloss adds that the strength may be referred to the bodily powers. On why the second is called like the first, he says the two are harmonious and mutually contain each other, since he who loves God loves his creature, and the chief of creatures is man; and he who loves an offending neighbour ought much more to love one always giving him benefits.

The scribe's reply is peculiar to this report. Ellicott observes that his words repeat the earlier compliment but without the covert sneer of the hypocrite, in the sincerity of admiration, an addition of singular interest, showing that some scribes accepted the spiritual meaning of the law; he hears in it the earnestness of conviction. Robertson takes the opening word as exclamatory: fine, Teacher, of a truth didst thou say. Calvin raises the objection the answer invites, that sacrifices belong to the worship of God and the first table, and should not be reckoned below charity to men; the worship of God is indeed preferable, he replies, but its outward exercises must not swallow up brotherly kindness, which is pleasing to God simply; and what is spoken of is naked and empty sacrifice, a hypocritical appearance of piety set against true uprightness.

On the verdict the voices divide by a hair. Theophylact insists it shows the man was not yet perfect, since it is not said he is within the kingdom but that he is not far from it. Pseudo-Jerome puts the same thing positively, that he is not far who comes with knowledge, since ignorance is farther from the kingdom than knowledge. Barnes takes it as evidence that a right understanding of the older law prepares the mind for the gospel, one system grafted on the other. Bede closes on the silence that follows: being confuted in argument they ask no further questions, but take him without disguise and give him up to the Roman power; the venom of envy may be overcome, but can hardly lie quiet.
35:
The counter-question is deliberate. Theophylact says that with the Passion approaching he corrects the opinion that the Christ was David's son and not his Lord, resting it on the source of the words: David cannot have spoken without the grace of the Holy Spirit. Pseudo-Jerome puts it bluntly: he speaks openly of himself so that they may be inexcusable. The Gloss sets the two propositions side by side: from David's words he is David's Lord, from the scribes' teaching his son. Bede takes the subjection of the enemies as showing not the Son's weakness but the unity of nature by which one works in the other, and finds the argument still useful against those who grant that the Christ is to come but make him a mere man of David's line; they are reproved not for calling him David's son but for not believing him the Son of God.

Henry turns it into a charge against the teachers. They told the people rightly that the Messiah was to be David's son, but could not tell how David then called him Lord. He draws two lessons: that the truths of God should be quoted from our Bibles rather than our ministers, the waters being sweetest drawn from their source, and that those are unworthy of Moses' seat who can preach the truth but cannot defend it.

How the crowd is described divides the modern voices. Barnes takes it of the poorer sort, since the rich and mighty were too proud to listen and it is so still; the fault is not the gospel's, for wherever there is a humble spirit, in rags or in purple, the blessings of salvation are conferred. Ellicott corrects the rendering to the great body of the people, the stress falling on the multitude and not their social condition. Robertson agrees it is the huge crowd, and notes that the attack begun that morning to destroy his influence had been a colossal failure, the crowds drawn closer than before. Henry is less confident of the gladness, noting that none is found wrought upon to follow him, so that he was to them a lovely song of one who plays well on an instrument; some may have cried crucify him afterwards, as Herod heard the Baptist gladly and yet cut off his head.

The warning that follows is bounded. Henry says the going in long clothing was not sinful but the loving to go in it and commanding respect by it. Bede agrees: he does not forbid that those whose office requires it should be saluted in the marketplace or given the chief seats, but teaches that those who love such things unduly are to be avoided, since it is the intention and not the office that is blamed; though it is culpable that men who wish to be called masters of the synagogue should be busy with lawsuits in the marketplace. He states the danger two ways: we should neither be seduced into thinking what they do good, nor be moved to imitate them by a vain pleasure in being praised for virtues they only affect.

On the widows' houses the three agree. Theophylact says they came to women left without their husbands' protection as though they were themselves protectors. Bede describes men who, pretending to be just, take money from persons troubled in conscience, as though they would be their advocates at the judgment; a hand stretched out to the poor should always accompany prayer, but these pass the night praying in order to take money from the poor. Henry guards the practice from the abuse: let fraud be thought the worse of for disguising itself in long prayers, but let not prayers be thought the worse of for being so abused; and since iniquity disguised as piety is double iniquity, its doom is doubly heavy, the damnation of hypocrites being the greatest of all.
41:
The setting comes before the act. Bede takes the word for treasury apart, a Greek verb meaning to keep joined to a Persian word for treasure, and notes it covered both the collecting chest and the porch where it stood. Theophylact adds the custom, that those able and willing put something in for the priests, the poor and the widows. On the coins the notes multiply. Clarke observes that even what the rich gave is called brass money, and names the smallest Jewish coin, two of which made a farthing; Robertson glosses the word for mite as peeled or stripped, and so very thin, and notes that the word for farthing is Latin, which Ellicott counts among the marks of this Gospel.

Two find the point in the setting rather than the sum. Ellicott says the position of the narrative gives it all the vividness of contrast: among the many who cast in much must have been some of those who devoured widows' houses, and here is a widow whose house had been devoured, showing by her act that she kept the two commandments the scribes had just set above all burnt offerings. Clarke supplies the rule that fixes her floor: the rabbis had a canon that none should put in less than two of these coins, so she could not have given less, and her poverty prevented her giving more. He adds that the notice of many rich casting in much may refer to the number of coins and not their value, and asks what we should think of a rich man throwing a handful of halfpence into a public collection.

The principle is stated three ways. Bede says God weighs not the property but the conscience of those who offer, considering not the sum but the store it came from. Barnes is careful about the comparison: it does not mean her gift was greater in value than the rest, but that it showed more love, self-denial and sincerity, the rule by which we shall be rewarded. Calvin draws it out both ways. The poor should not hesitate to give cheerfully out of slender means, since an offering that looks worthless will not be less valuable than all the treasures of Croesus; and the rich are reminded that a moderate sum out of a vast heap is of less value in God's sight than a very little that exhausts a poor man's store. The chief sacrifice God requires, he adds, is self-denial.

Calvin also refuses to let the abuse of the treasury spoil the act: the offerings were probably not applied to lawful purposes then, but the service of the law was still in force, and men's abuses could not prevent sincere worshippers from doing what was holy. Robertson observes that what she cast in was her livelihood rather than her life; it is a tragedy, he says, to see a stingy saint pose as giving the widow's mite when he could give thousands instead of pennies.

The allegories are three and do not agree. Bede makes the rich the Jews puffed up with the righteousness of the law and the widow the simplicity of the Church, poor because she has cast away pride, widowed because her husband suffered death for her; her two mites are the love of God and of neighbour, and she sends her whole living, knowing it is not her own desert but divine grace. Theophylact makes the widow the soul, which leaves the Satan it was joined to and casts in flesh and mind, the flesh by abstinence and the mind by humility. Pseudo-Jerome puts himself in the parable: the rich bring out of the heart's treasure things new and old, and who is the poor woman, he asks, if not himself and those like him, who cast in what they can and have the will to explain where they have not the power.
